content: Seizures occurring after a stroke represent a significant clinical issue, often leading to unfavorable outcomes. The role of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) in preventing seizures following a stroke remains uncertain. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of AEDs in both primary and secondary prevention of post-stroke seizures. For primary prevention, the goal was to determine whether AEDs could reduce the likelihood of seizures in individuals who had experienced a stroke but had not yet had a seizure. For secondary prevention, the focus was on whether AEDs could decrease the risk of recurrent seizures in individuals who had already experienced at least one seizure after a stroke. A comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted on March 9, 2021, including sources such as the Cochrane Register of Studies, MEDLINE, PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and others. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials involving participants with a clinical diagnosis of stroke, either ischemic or hemorrhagic. Studies focusing solely on subarachnoid, subdural, or extradural hemorrhages, or non-stroke-related conditions such as tumors or infections, were excluded. Participants of all ages and seizure types were included, provided they were assigned to either AED or placebo groups. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted relevant data. The primary outcome was the proportion of participants who experienced seizures during the follow-up period. Results were presented as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs for continuous outcomes. Meta-analyses were performed when sufficient data were available, and statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. The GRADE approach was employed to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. Two studies, involving a total of 856 participants, were included in the review. The evidence did not support the effectiveness of AEDs for primary prevention of post-stroke seizures (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.26; moderate-certainty evidence). The first study was a randomized, double-blind trial comparing valproic acid to placebo for up to one year after stroke in 72 adults with intracerebral hemorrhage. No significant difference was observed in the risk of post-stroke seizures (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.35 to 2.16) or mortality (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.40 to 3.58). The second study was a randomized, double-blind trial evaluating a three-day course of diazepam versus placebo for primary seizure prevention in 784 adults with acute stroke. No significant difference was found in the risk of post-stroke seizures for all stroke types or subgroups of hemorrhagic or ischemic stroke (RR for all stroke 0.47, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.22). However, in a subgroup analysis of anterior circulation cortical infarcts, diazepam was associated with a reduced risk of post-stroke seizures (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.95). Mortality rates did not differ between the diazepam and placebo groups at two weeks (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.26) or three months (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.26). Both studies were assessed to have a low overall risk of bias, and the certainty of the evidence was rated as low to moderate using the GRADE approach. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of AEDs for the primary or secondary prevention of seizures following a stroke. Further high-quality studies are needed to address this clinically significant issue.
